recent.narrative: Blizzard conditions developed in Kotzebue late in the morning of the 1st as the surface low moved through the Bering Strait. Winds died down in the evening as the low moved away resulting in improved visibility. Winds in Kotzebue gusted as high as 44 mph during the event.

Blizzard conditions developed on the Baldwin Peninsula and Selawik Valley the morning of the 25th and continued into the in early morning hours of the 26th. Winds at Kotzebue gusted as high as 67 mph. Noorvik had wind gusts to 58 mph and Selawik had gusts to 45 mph.

Blizzard conditions developed on on the Baldwin Peninsula on the morning of the 4th and continued through the morning of the 6th. Winds gusted as high as 52 mph during the event. The strong winds caused a citywide power outage in Kotzebue, which subsequently  caused the city's water system to fail. Significant drifting caused made travel in Kotzebue difficult for several days after the event.
Selawik AWOS had multiple hours of low visibility, gusty winds, and heavy snow with conditions as low as quarter mile visibility and winds gusting up to 45 MPH.

Both Noorvik and Kotzebue reported numerous hours of heavy snow, visibilities less than a quarter mile and strong winds. Noorvik had wind gusts up to 53 MPH while Kotzebue had gusts as high as 54 mph. The storm left residents in Kotzebue without power which also caused the city's water plant to shut down.
Kotzebue Police Department estimated 4-6 with peak of event showing visibility reduced to a quarter mile and gusting to 49 knots.

recent.narrative: Two observation sites in Whittier began reporting west winds sustained at 30 to 35 mph gusting between 40 and 50 mph with 1/4 mile visibility or less between 6 am and 7 am AKST 4/9, lasting close to 24 hours until 6 am AKST 4/10 as winds began to diminish.  This was also supported by local webcam imagery that showed very poor visibility beginning around the same time and lasting for many hours.

The Portage Glacier Center ASOS recorded 1/4 mile visibility in heavy snow and frequent gusts 35+ mph from 8:44 AM - 11:53 AM. While, visibility was reduced to 1/4 or 1/2 mile due to heavy snow in many locations, no other stations saw prolonged periods of 1/4 mile vis with winds 35+ mph. ||- Alaska DOT reported difficult driving conditions along Seward Hwy from Indian Road, all the way to Seward. Whiteout conditions described on Alyeska Highway. Atmospheric conditions described as Winter Storm from Seward Hwy at Ingram Creek to Hope Y, with very difficult conditions (Travel is not advised) for Turnagain Arm. ||- Multiple reports of whiteout conditions, vehicles in ditches along Seward Hwy road conditions Facebook groups. Several posts were made about the blizzard warning in these groups.

Alaska DOT reported blizzard and whiteout conditions with snow amounts ranging from 6-24 inches. Chugach Avalanche Center Meteorologist, Wendy Wagner, reported multiple cars in the ditch, including a police vehicle, as well as, 18 inches on the road at the top of the pass. The verifying ASOS report noted quarter mile visibility, heavy snowfall and peak wind gusts of 34 kts at 12:44pm March 18, 2023.

Blizzard conditions were observed by the Whittier MAWS from the morning of March 1 through early afternoon. Visibility was 1/4 miles or less, with winds gusting in excess of 35 knots (40 mph). Visibility improved by the afternoon and evening as the intensity of snowfall decreased.

Webcam images from Whittier tunnel staging area showed widespread low visibilities with snow and blowing snow during daylight hours on 2/10.  The Portage AWOS reported 1/4 mile visibility snow and blowing snow between about 10 AM and 6 PM AKST 2/10.

The Portage AWOS recorded strong easterly winds gusting to around 45 MPH with light to moderate snow and blowing snow, with visibility reduced to 1/2 mile or less between about 10 AM and 5 PM AKST 2/5.  The Chugach National Forest Avalanche Center also reported 1/2 mile visibility or less at times with 6 inches of new snowfall and wind gusting between 25 and 35 mph at 2 PM AKST the same day.

Blizzard conditions developed in Nome for several hours in the late morning hours of the 25th. In the early afternoon, conditions improved briefly; however, blizzard conditions returned in late afternoon and continued through the evening hours. Nome had gusts as high as 41 mph during the event while Golovin had gusts as high as 53 mph.

Winds began to increase late in the evening of the 19th as the front approached from the south. Blizzard conditions develop in Nome the morning of the 20th as snow moved into the area. The visibility improved as the winds died down late in the afternoon. The winds in both Nome and Golovin gusted as high as 54 mph during the event, while winds gusted as high as 52 mph in White Mountain.

Blizzard conditions developed along the southern coast of the Seward Peninsula on the on the morning of the 4th, first at Nome and then at Golovin. The visibility improved in Nome by the evening of the 4th; however, in Golovin periods of blizzard conditions continued into the afternoon of the 5th. Winds during the event peaked at 43 mph in Golovin and 41 mph in Nome.
Nome ASOS reported reported multiple hours of heavy snow and gusty winds reducing visibility to quarter mile or less at times. Peak wind gusts were as high as 39 MPH.
Nome ASOS had multiple hours of heavy snow, gusty winds, and quarter mile visibilities from blowing snow. The ASOS reported peak winds gusts up to 45 MPH.
Golovin AWOS reported a 62 mph wind gust and was the peak for the event the morning of the 23rd. Winds continued in the area before tapering off early afternoon on the 25th.

Two separate measurements of wind gusts to 81 mph were recorded from Saint George and Saint Paul Island on the morning of 9/17.  The gust to 81 mph on Saint Paul was recorded by the PASN AWOS at 8:45 AM AKST, and the gust to 81 mph on Saint George was recorded at 9:41 AKST.  School was cancelled on the island of Saint Paul due to the high winds on 9/17.

The Saint Paul ASOS recorded a 3 hour period of blizzard conditions on the evening of March 28. Winds gusted as high as 38 knots (44 mph) while blowing snow led to one quarter mile visibility. Conditions improved quickly after 10 pm AKDT as precipitation came to an end.

The Saint Paul ASOS did not report visibility during this event. Winds gusted 35 knots (40 mph) or greater with whiteout conditions seen on FAA webcam imagery between 10 am and 2 pm on March 18, during which temperatures were also below freezing. At 6 pm, an NWS employee at the Saint Paul Weather Service Office measured between 4 to 6 inches of snow from the event.
A mesonet observation in Saint Paul recorded a wind gust to 70 knots (81 mph) around 2 AM on February 28 as a low pressure system in the Bering Sea passed north of the island near peak intensity.

The Saint Paul AWOS began reporting blizzard to near blizzard conditions starting at around 8 am 2/15 as the front approached from the west, and lasted through about 3 pm that same afternoon.  The highest winds gusted to 59 mph as the front approached at about 1 PM 2/15.

Blizzard conditions with significant snow and blowing snow occurred from 9:35 AM through 7:20 PM on February 13th at the Saint George AWOS. Visibility remained between 1/4 to 1/2 mile until February 14th at 2:00 AM. Winds peaked between approximately 3 PM to 6 PM February 13th, with sustained winds up to 56 mph and gusts up to 63 mph.
Kyle Sobek (Thompson Pass DOT) reported 2 to 2 1/2 feet storm total snow at Thompson Pass and 10 in Tonsina.

The Thompson Pass DOT camp reported that their highest observed wind gust was 96 mph at camp. They also reported that the wind gusts were much stronger through the Thompson Pass gap. Meanwhile, the Valdez ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 76 mph.
DOT reported that wind gusts reached 75 mph around 2:00 am along with heavy drifting snow in and near the Gap, while visibility reduced to 1 mile.

As the front passed through Prince William Sound, it spread a heavy mix of rain and snow along and ahead of the front. The rain/snow mix mostly affected the coastline, while heavy and blowing snow created blizzard conditions along the mountains and mountain passes. DOT reported hazardous road conditions with heavy snow, whiteout conditions due to both heavy snow and blowing snow, and heavy drifting through Thompson Pass as snow amounts of 8 to 16 inches were noted and winds maxed out at 55 mph. Gareth with the Valdez Avalanche Center reported 20 from the summit of the pass north towards the Copper River Basin. Towards Valdez, heavy snow transitioned to a heavy mix from mile 20 through Keystone Canyon, which created very difficult to hazardous driving conditions. Snow transitioned to heavy rain from the Canyon towards Valdez.
Alaska 511 reported whiteout conditions with poor visibility and snow on December 25th at 1127PM.

Temperatures initially rose with the arrival of a cold, dense airmass during the early morning hours of December 23 as northeasterly winds vertically mixed warmer air aloft down to the surface across Northeastern Prince William Sound. However, colder air gradually worked in throughout the day, allowing temperatures to fall. The Alaska Department of Transportation reported 25 to 45 mph winds through Thompson Pass, causing wind chills below -40F by December 24. Winds diminished late on December 24, ending the cold wind chills.
Blizzard conditions developed at Barter Island on the evening of the 8th and continued through the morning of the 9th. Winds gusted as high as 54 mph at Barter Island during the event.
Point Thompson AWOS reported -36F, 15 MPH, and wind chills as low as -72F.

Blizzard conditions developed at Barter Island on the morning of the 1st and lasted into early in the day on the 2nd. Barter Island saw wind gusts as high as 55 mph from the southeast during this event.
Blizzard conditions occurred at both Barter Island and Point Thomson. The strongest winds occurred on Barter Island where winds gusted as high as 60 mph.
Point Thomson reported wind chill values colder than -60 degrees Fahrenheit for over 24 hours, with -63 degrees Fahrenheit being the coldest value reported.
Barter Island reported wind chill values as cold as -69 degrees Fahrenheit.

The Mekoryuk ASOS (PAMY) reported heavy snowfall, winds gusting to over 40 mph, and visibility below one quarter of a mile from 8:55 PM AKST March 8th to 1:45 AM AKST March 9th. Webcams overlooking the village comfirmed this heavy snowfall and low visiblity.

The Mekoryuk ASOS station (PAMY) reported 0 to quarter mile visibilities and winds gusting to the mid 40s for several hours from 7:30 AM AKST to 2:30 PM AKST on January 30th. Multiple webcams along the coast from Newtok to Goodnews Bay revealed whiteout conditions in the morning hours of January 30th.

The Mekoryuk ASOS Station (PAMY) reported heavy snow, gusty winds over 40 mph and visibility below one quarter of a mile from 10:44 AM AKST to past 2:30 PM AKST on January 26th. Webcams in the village confirmed this low visibility. Nunapitchuk Airport (PPIT) similarly reported blizzard conditions with winds gusting to 45 to 50 mph and quarter mile visibility from 9:20 PM AKST January 26 to 12:00 AM AKST January 27.

Below average sea ice extent, including shorefast ice, was insufficient to properly shelter communities along the Kuskokwim Delta coast from storm surge. A Kwigillingok community coordinator shared pictures showcasing flooding that occurred on January 12th. Flooding continued into January 13th, coinciding with the high tide. The community leader noted that water levels were worse than a recent flooding event that took place on January 10th.

Kwigillingok, Alaska saw major flooding on January 10th. A tribal resilience coordinator reported that water levels were the highest ... seen thus far. He continued: A group of Russian Orthodox Christians, observing Slaviq (a Russian Orthodox equivalent to Christmas), were forced to stay put in a house because there were numerous spots too deep to cross on boardwalks. Snow machine trails were all water as well. A search and rescue worker reported 4 - 8 ft of water. An article from Alaska Public Media reported that the Native Village of Kwigillingok Tribal Administrator noted that multiple boardwalks were submerged in the lower part of the community. Alaska Public Media article link: https://alaskapublic.org/2025-01-13/tidal-action-and-fierce-winds-flood-low-lying-areas-of-kwigillingok.

A tide gage in Kwigillingok measured water levels exceeding 2.3 feet above mean higher high water (MHHW) between December 18th and 19th. A local Tribal Resilience Office reported that lakes in Kwigillingok overflowed with standing water near the village. A dirt road in the village was inundated, but most elevated walkways avoided flooding. There were isolated cases of flooding over boardwalks in low-lying areas. There was an ice jam along small creeks and sloughs in the vicinity of the village. A Tribal Official in Kipnuk reported that lakes were overflowing around the village. There were isolated cases of water rising up and over portions of boardwalks in low-lying areas. Water levels in Kipnuk began rising around 4:00 to 5:00 AM AKST on December 19th. Winds during this period was southeasterly at around 23 mph and gusting to 35 mph.

The Cape Newenham ASOS station (PAEH) observed 0 to quarter mile visibilities with winds gusting to over 55 mph from 9:00 AM AKST January 30th to 1:00 AM AKST January 31st. Webcams in Goodnews Bay revealed near whiteout conditions at 10:30 AM on January 30th.

Local observations noted 3 hours of 1/4SM +SN or less with winds gusting 32 kt or greater beginning 030228Z, peaking at 44kts. Winds dropped out at PAPM during the worst conditions, with higher gusts having been likely. Winds diminished gradually as snow tapered off leading to improving visibility just after midnight.

The Port Heiden AWOS reported just over three hours of blizzard conditions on the afternoon of March 30. Visibility remained at or below one quarter mile while winds gusted as high as 39 knots (45 mph). Blizzard-like conditions were observed along the Bering Sea coast of the Alaska Peninsula as far north as Naknek, though this occurred for a shorter time period. The Pilot Point AWOS stopped reporting shortly after the onset of blizzard-like conditions, so it is unknown for how long the conditions lasted there.

The Koliganek AWOS recorded 1/2 mile or lower visibility with 25 to 30 mph winds in snow and blowing snow between 9:30 AM and 1:20 PM AKST 2/21.  Temperatures warmed to or above 32 degrees Fahrenheit later in the afternoon, allowing blowing snow to end.

An NWS Meteorological Technician in King Salmon reported 6 inches of new snowfall over a 12 hour period between 9 PM February 19th and 9 AM February 20th.  The King Salmon AWOS also recorded 0.93 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation during this timeframe, adding further support to the estimated new snowfall reported.

NWS Anchorage called out to several communities across Bristol Bay after and during the heavy snowfall event.  The Togiak city office estimated up to 2 feet of snow fell in a little over a day between 12 PM 2/14 and 1 PM 2/15, resulting in a hour long delay in starting school the morning of 2/15.  The Dillingham police department estimated a total of 4 to 8 inches had fallen ending at 3 PM AKST on 2/14, and the office was advising their employees to go home early due to the heavy snow ongoing at the time.  The Port Heiden city office estimated about 6 to 7 inches of new snowfall since yesterday at 1 PM 2/15.

Blizzard conditions developed late in the evening of the 24th and continued into the evening of the 25th along the western Arctic Coast.  Cape Lisburne had wind gusts as high as 100 mph while Wainwright had wind gusts as high as 50 mph.

Point Lay reported several hours of blizzard conditions. Blizzard conditions developed early in the morning hours and continued into the evening. The blizzard conditions at Point Lay were accompanied by wind gusts as high as 51 mph. Elsewhere, Wainwright reported strong winds all day with as high as 54 mph. The visibility in Wainwright was under a one mile for most of the day due to blowing snow, with the visibility occasionally dropping to as low as one quarter mile.

Blizzard conditions developed in Utqiagvik during the early morning hours of the 24th and continued through the late morning. The blizzard conditions were accompanied by wind gusts as high as 55 mph in Utqiagvik.
Point Lay AWOS reported multiple hours of quarter mile visibility with wind gusts as high as 45 MPH and heavy snow.
Point Lay AWOS reported wind chills as low as -69F.
Point Lay AWOS reported 35 MPH with wind chills as low as -65F.

Strong winds developed along the Beaufort Sea coast the morning of the 15th. Nuiqsut saw gusts as high as 42 mph while Deadhorse saw gusts as high as 35 mph. The strong winds caused blowing snow to develop at both locations with several hours where the visibility below one quarter mile.
The Deadhorse airport reported gusts to 35 mph with visibility less than one quarter mile for just over three hours.
Deadhorse reported gusts as high as 60 mph with visibility less than one quarter mile. The blizzard conditions persisted for over 24 hours.
Kuparuk reported wind chill values colder than -60 for over 24 hours with -68 degrees Fahrenheit being the coldest value reported.
Kuparuk reported wind chill values as cold a -78 degrees Fahrenheit.

Temperatures in the -30's F along the eastern Arctic coast combined with southwest winds around 15 mph resulted in bitterly cold wind chill readings.  The Deadhorse airport reported wind chill temperatures to -64 F.

Blizzard conditions developed on the Bering Strait coast early in the morning, of the 16th and continued into the early evening. Blizzard conditions were reported at both Brevig Mission and Wales. Brevig Mission had two distinct periods of blizzard conditions during this event, with blizzard conditions present for much of the morning, with a second shorter period in the evening. Wales reported blizzard conditions for much of the morning of the 16th. Brevig Mission reported a peak wind gust of 48 mph during the event, while the peak wind gust at Wales was 41 mph.

High winds developed along the Bering Strait Coast as well as St. Lawrence Island on the evening of May 13th and continued into the early morning hours of May 14th. Teller reported wind gusts as high as 76 mph during this event. Wales reported gusts as high as 62 mph before the wind sensor failed during the middle of the event. Elsewhere, Tin City reported wind gusts as high as 60 mph, while Brevig Mission reported gusts as high as 59 mph and Gambell reported gusts as high as 52 mph.

Blizzard conditions developed along the Bering Strait Coast the morning of the 25th and continued through at least the evening of the 25th. Winds were gusting to 71 mph at Teller when the AWOS stopped reporting data for the event. Elsewhere during the event, Tin City had gusts to 64 mph and Brevig Mission had gusts to 61 mph.

Winds began to increase the evening of the 19th as the front approached the St. Lawrence Island and the Bering Strait Coast. Blizzard conditions developed as snow associated with the front began falling just after midnight on the 20th, with blizzard conditions continuing through the early morning hours of the 21st. During the event, winds gusted as high as 67 mph at Gambell, 67 mph at Tin City, 60 mph at Teller, 59 mph at Savoonga and 45 mph at Bervig Mission.

Blizzard conditions developed in the early morning hours of the 4th on both St. Lawrence Island and the coast of the Bering Strait and continued through midday on the 5th. Winds at Savoonga gusted as high as 71 mph. Other peak wind gusts include: 69 mph at Tin City, 67 mph at Teller, 54 mph at Gambell and 41 mph at Brevig Mission.
Brevig Mission AWOS reported multiple hours of heavy snow and low visibility, as low as a quarter mile at times and wind gusts as high as 52 MPH.

The Global Lightning Detection Network and daily lightning summary from the Alaska Inter-agency Coordination Center and Bureau of Land Management showed numerous lightning strikes across much of the Copper River Basin during the afternoon and evening of 7/24. This lightning occurred for several hours in intense thunderstorms observed on satellite and radar, with one thunderstorm cell moving into the area of greater concern for drier fire fuels over Glennallen and Gulkana late at night on 7/24, or right around 12 am AKST 7/25.  In spite of this, no new fire starts were reported.

Borderline Red Flag conditions at the Gulkana ASOS began at 2:53 pm AKST and continued through 6:00 pm AKST. Temperatures ranged from 70 to 72 Fahrenheit. South winds ranged from 10 to 17 mph with a peak gust of 24 mph. Relative humidity ranged from 18 to 22%. A few other nearby mesonet observations reported temperatures between 70 and 75 between 2:30 pm AKST and 7:30 pm AKST with winds around 15 mph and relative humidity values of 18 to 22%.

Numerous reports of accumulating snowfall were relayed by the Alaska Department of Transportation, most of which fell from about 11 PM 5/30 to the early morning hours of 5/31.  Around 6 inches fell over Glennallen, with mostly 1-2 inches of slush reported farther south and west.  Heavier snowfall was reported along the Tok Cutoff and northern Richardson Highway, including up to 10 inches in Paxson.

DOT reported 10 inches new snow in Tonsina. Meanwhile, the 511 webpage noted very difficult road conditions from MM 42 to 82 along the Richardson Hwy due to heavy snow, wind, blowing snow, drifting snow, icy patches, and reduced visibility.

A member of the public estimated that 6 inches of snow fell near Willow Lake. Several other estimates around 4-5 inches south of Glenallen along the Edgerton Highway, as well as near Eureka. Snow began on the morning of March 1 and largely ended by the evening hours. Some upslope snow showers with light accumulations continued beyond this point in the western portions of the Copper River Basin.

Alaska Department of Transportation reported a myriad of mixed precipitation starting out as snow, then mostly transitioning to rain as warm air above freezing filtered into valleys across the Copper River Basin from the south with time between 1/24 and 1/25.  Most locations did not receive significant snowfall or rainfall totals (no more than 6-7 inches of new snowfall prior to transition). Tazlina reported a brief period of freezing rain before switching over from snow to all rain during at around 5 AM 1/25.

Red Flag Warning (pre-greenup) criteria at the Palmer ASOS began at 2:15 pm AKST and continued through 6:00 pm AKST. Temperatues ranged from 72 to 74 Fahrenheit. Southeast winds ranged from 15 mph to 25 mph with a peak gust of 33 mph. Relative humidity ranged from 22% to 25% during this same time period.

The AWOS in Wasilla reported unknown precipitation type at around 4 PM AKST, verified to be mainly freezing rain based on other reports and nearby webcam imagery.  The Glenn Highway was reportedly very slick south of the Parks Highway and Glenn Highway interchange near Palmer during the same afternoon and evening.

Surface observations indicated blowing snow began around midnight on December 23 as northeasterly gap winds rapidly developed and conditions worsened through the day. Winds were sustained at around 40 knots (46 mph) at both the Palmer and Wasilla surface observing sites for nearly 21 hours from the early morning through nearly midnight. Wind gusts reached 71 knots (82 mph) at the peak of the event (405 PM December 23) as observed by the Palmer ASOS. Blizzard conditions were most widespread and were recorded at both the ASOS in Palmer and the AWOS in Wasilla around midday December 23. The Wasilla AWOS stopped reporting any data during the peak of the event. ||This wind event was exacerbated by the amount of snow on the ground; snow that had fallen earlier in the month. Ground blizzard conditions were noted at several area weather stations as snow and blowing snow, as well as visibilities

A third round of heavy snow occurred December 14 through 15 resulting in about a foot of snow across the Matanuska Valley, on top of the snowfall still on the ground from the previous two December snowfall events, leading to increased impacts across the Valley. This snowfall was produced as a tropical moisture plume spread northward and combined with an upper-level disturbance transitioning across the state. The bulk of the snowfall arrived late Wednesday afternoon and continued through Thursday morning. Unlike the last two snow events, snow fell in a more uniform manner. The verifying observation came in from Big Lake where 16 inches of new snow were measured over a 12 hour period.

The second round of heavy snow occurred on December 11 through 12 resulting in 1 to 2 feet of snow across the Borough. Reports of snowfall measured ranged from 12 to 24 inches across the Matanuska Valley. The verifying report came in from Palmer with 24 inches of new snow measured within 24 hours.

Most of the heavier snowfall fell between the evening of 12/6/22 and the morning of 12/7.  Storm total snowfall reports from public, spotters and NWS employees ranged from about 10 inches to 16 inches across the Matanuska Valley, with the highest amounts focused between Big Lake and Wasilla. The Big Lake, Wasilla, Goat Creek, and Knik River areas were hit with numerous power outages in connection with the heavy snowfall on the morning of 12/7.

A SNOTEL located in McNeil Canyon Reported 17 inches of snow in 24 hours (12/12 4:00 AM AKST to 12/13 4:00 AM AKST). On the evening of the 12th, A NOAA Oceanographer in Homer reported that a foot of snow had fallen in McNeil Canyon by 10 AM on the 13th and 10 inches of snow had fallen in the BayCrest area of the Homer Bluffs by 12/12 5:30 PM AKST. In Homer proper, only a few inches of slushy snowfall had fallen by the end of the event on the 13th.

A social media post reported a storm total measurement of 16 inches in Ninilchik between 9 AM AKST 11/3 and 1 PM AKST 11/4/24.  Several other snowfall reports of 5 to 12 inches were noted across the Homer Bluffs and along the Sterling Highway between Homer and Ninilchik between 11/3 and 11/4.  At least two vehicles went off the road while heavy snowfall was occurring in the area.

A public report of 9 inches total snowfall was received shortly before 5 PM AKST 2/4 near Nikiski.  Numerous other reports ranging from 6 to 9 inches of new snowfall were received across the rest of the western Kenai Peninsula between 2/3 and 2/4.

Thunderstorms developing off the Western Alaska Range in the afternoon on June 17 pushed west over the Lower Kuskokwim Valley, producing numerous lightning strikes. Thunderstorm activity lasted through around 10 pm. A total of 17 new fire starts in the Southwest region were reported in Alaska Interagency Coordination Center situation report on June 18.

The Sleetmute AWOS reported 0.04 inches of freezing rain from 3 to 7 am on November 24. A strong upper-level trough tracking northwest across Southwest Alaska produced widespread showers and warmed temperatures aloft above freezing. Prior to this, light showers produced only snow in the Lower Kuskokwim Valley east of Aniak. Temperatures remained 32 or below in Sleetmute for all of November 24.
Sleetmute, AK Post Office reported 4-6 inches of snow.

Several weather observing sites across the Lower Kuskokwim Valley reported periods of 1/2 mile visibility or less due to moderate/blowing snow. A member of the public reported difficult travel conditions due to blowing snow and reduced visibility in Aniak.

A member of the public measured 6.8 inches of snowfall accumulation in Eagle River. Snow began in the morning on February 28 and ended by the afternoon.

Intermittent moderate snowfall continued through the night with another 2 inches falling, but the total compressing down to 7.5 inches. The nearby COOP measured 6 inches from this event. At approximately 1pm AKDT on the 22nd, reports starting coming in of significant blow down of trees and damage in the community of Elfin Cove. The local COOP/Emergency Manager reported that at least 5 homes had large trees through their roof and a treefall/rockslide took out part of the power line. Strongest winds occurred around 11am AKDT with a sudden wind shift from east to west and gusts estimated around 70mph.||The Governor of State of Alaska declared a disaster declaration for this event. The State Emergency Operations Center reported: 15 homes with some damage, a cell tower destroyed, phone building with major damage, major damage to radio repeaters, an impassable boardwalk due to downed trees and a 10���15 ft section as unsafe due to structural damage. Estimate expense by the state was $300 thousand, but a value of exact property damage is unknown. ||The ferry M/V Columbia travel

Pelican COOP measured 5.3 inches of snow at their morning measurement on the 30th, with snowfall rates likely picking up after. Start and end times are estimated based on surrounding areas and snow ending in the evening. Therefore, with the COOP measurement of 2.7 inches the following morning, 8 inches of snow fell in approximately 19 hours. Overall totals were greater than this due to snow that had occurred the day before.

The Pelican COOP measured 2.4 inches of snow by 8am on the 27th and another 8.1 inches by the following morning. Based on other communities nearby, greatest snowfall rates were likely during the day on the 27th.

A spotter in Pelican reported on social media that there was flying debris and trees down, along with roofing coming loose in places and windows blown out. Later a COOP observer in Pelican reported 67 mph wind gusts were measured at his personal weather station and reported that a roof was coming off of a building and windows had been blown out.

A COOP observer measured a storm total of 18.8 inches of snow from a multi-day snowfall event. The snowfall was heaviest January 22nd and early on the 23rd when a 24 hour amount of 11.5 inches was measured, before an eventual changeover to rain occurred later that night.

The Pelican COOP Observer measured 13.3 inches of snow had fallen by 8am on the 13th, another 14.5 inches by 8am on the 14th and another 4.7 inches on the 15th when it had changed to rain. A few more inches of additional snow fell on the 16th brining nearly 3 feet of snow to the community over the MLK long weekend event.

The Hoonah COOP reported damaging winds on the 17th, noting: heavy gusts, fallen trees, power outages, light shelters destroyed, and debris on road. After 8am that day the Hoonah Airport AWOS stopped reporting due to a power outage caused by a tree in the lines, which was confirmed later by the local power company with photos.

Hoonah COOP measured 3.6 inches of snow at 730am on the 30th. The airport AWOS was not reporting during this time, making start and end times estimated, but surrounding areas reported snowfall rates increase after the morning COOP report and ended in the evening. Therefore the COOP measurement of 9.1 inches at 8am on the 31st fell in approximately 12 hours.

Snow is estimated to have begun around midnight on the 1st with the Hoonah COOP measuring 5.5 inches by 8am. The COOP measured another 12.2 inches by 7am on the 2nd when moderate rain at 32 degrees was observed.

The Hoonah AWOS station at the airport measured temperatures at or below 32 degrees between midnight and 6am with a minimum of 28 degrees the morning of the 1st. The Hoonah COOP in town also recorded a minimum temperature of 32 degrees that morning.

A public comment on social media reported 7 inches already in Hoonah by 7am on the 27th. The Hoonah COOP station at the water treatment plan measured 12 inches of snow by 9am along with very poor visibility. The COOP measured another 4.8 inches by the following morning. Other social media reports in Hoonah noted an estimated 18 inches in under 6 hours and another shared a photo of 2 feet as of 1235pm with snow continuing to fall heavily. The Hoonah airport was reporting gusts of 20-30 mph and visibility down to a quarter mile.

Light snow began during the day on the 12th with rates picking up overnight. The Hoonah COOP measured 7.4 inches by 820am the next morning. Snow became lighter through the 13th and didn't add up much more due to compression over the next 2 days. Over the MLK long weekend (3.5 days), a total of 12.9 inches fell in Hoonah, but most of that occurred by Saturday morning the 13th, as noted above.

The public reported hearing a loud, thunder-like, sound around 7am AKDT Wednesday near downtown Juneau and Douglas, which was later determined to be a stack of shipping containers being blown over at the AML dock. At 813am the power company reported an outage north of town and the public reported trees down in the same area. Within the next hour, siding was reported blown off an apartment building and a large wooden playset blown over in the Mendenhall Valley. At 1122am AKDT, a very strong gust caused an area-wide power outage. Within the 11am hour, elevation sites around Juneau peaked at 78-85mph. The peak gust recorded at the Juneau Airport ASOS during this event was 53mph at 122pm AKDT.

The landslide generated tsunami scoured trees and vegetation from both sides of the Tracy Arm fjord. The National Tsunami Warning Center reported that the maximum tsunami wave height at the Juneau tide gauge was 36 cm (approximately 14 in) from the normal tide prediction, which occurred around outgoing and low tide, and continued to measure successive waves for 5 hours.

Public reports through the morning of the 30th showed heavy snow on Douglas Island that had accumulated to 6 inches overnight, some of that likely included lighter snow that had fallen during the day before. Heavy snow continued over this portion of the Juneau Borough through the 30th with a measurement of 15 inches at lower elevations of West Juneau by 304pm. The school district use the snow bus routes for Douglas and cancelled afternoon activities. Other parts of Juneau saw much less, totaling 5 to 9 inches of snow in the Valley and out the road between the 28th and 31st of January.

Snow began just before midnight on December 1st at the Juneau airport and quickly became heavy. A social media report noted that 6 inches of snow had already fallen by 6am near the airport and another report of up to 10 inches on Douglas Island by 1245pm. Snow continued through Sunday evening, then saw several hours of sleet then several hours of freezing rain through the following morning. Rain continued to fall on the snowpack, causing localized flooding and icy conditions. Schools were closed on Monday the 2nd and city offices had a delay. Storm totals from the event ranged from 10 to 17.5 inches of snow with an eighth inch glaze of ice.

Light snow fell across the Juneau area throughout the daytime on Nov. 26th with 3 to 5 inches reported, some of which included snow from the previous evening. Snowfall rates then increased through the night of the 26th with an average of 3 inches measured in each 6 hour period between 3pm to 9am the following morning, reaching 9 inches in that 18 hour period.

Mesonet station at the top of the Juneau Library recorded a peak wind gust of 74mph at 442am on the 22nd. Multiple other Marine Exchange of Alaska stations recorded high winds during the time frame, with frequent gusts over the high wind criteria of 60mph.

costliest.narrative: Light and very dry snow began to fall the evening of Friday January 12th. After 9pm, rates increased and by 8am the Juneau Waste Water Treatment Plant COOP measured 7 inches of snow and similar amounts were measured at the NWS Weather Forecast Office in the Mendenhall Valley and near Lena Point that morning as well. Snow continued to fall through Saturday with several more inches accumulating then changed to freezing drizzle Sunday morning. This compacted the snow from the day before and created an icy crust. By late Sunday morning precipitation changed back to snow and began to add up again. Snowfall rates were very heavy throughout the Monday holiday and density of the the snow was wet and difficult to move. Storm total snowfall at the NWS Office was 33.1 inches and an NWS employee on North Douglas measured a storm total of 38 inches. ||An avalanche occurred around 6pm Monday along Tha

recent.narrative: The Hydaburg AWOS measured wind gusts trending up through the day on the 19th, peaking at 56mph at 519pm AKST. The AWOS station stopped reporting after 552pm, likely due to a power outage. The Klawock COOP observer noted damaging wind had occurred on both the 19th and 20th in their 9am report. On the other side of the island, the FAA webcam near Kasaan measured sustained winds in excess of 40mph between 220-420pm on the 19th, including a peak sustained wind speed of 47mph.
The Hydaburg AWOS measured high winds for several hours early on November 9th, including a peak gust of 68mph at 558am.

A social media report estimated wind gusts to 65mph at Coffman Cove all day on the 26th. Another social media comment estimated 70mph gusts in Port Protection at the northern end of Prince of Wales Island shortly after 3pm AKDT. Peak wind measured at the Hydaburg AWOS was 51kt (59mph) at 852am AKDT. A lightning strike that morning disabled the automated system at the City of Klawock's water treatment plant. The Craig COOP observer estimated wind gusts of 60mph at their morning report and checked the damaging wind box. The Klawock COOP also checked the damaging wind box on the 26th.
Hydaburg AWOS measured a peak gust of 51 knots (59mph) at 251am and 307am AKDT. The Klawock COOP marked damaging wind in their morning report.

COOP observer in Craig and Klawock noted damaging wind in their 8am report on the 17th. Craig Police confirmed that fallen trees caused brown outs in Craig and power outages resulting in a fire in two other communities on Prince of Wales Island between the hours of 4am and 8am AKDT. There was also a report of roof damage in Craig. Peak winds measured in Craig was 57mph at 424am AKDT.

The Hydaburg Seaplane Base AWOS started measuring gusts above 60mph at 420am on the 26th and continued through mid-day, including a peak gust of 81mph at 509am. A social media report shared a photo of damage to a porch roof from this event. Other peak winds across Prince of Wales Island ranged from a 57mph gust in Craig to sustained winds of 54mph at the Kasaan FAA webcam. The Inter Island Ferry was cancelled for the day in anticipation of the storm.

The Marine Exchange station at Salmon Landing in Ketchikan briefly measured high winds during the afternoon of the 9th, including a peak gust of 64mph at 144pm AKST. Another station at Saxman measured a peak gust of 62mph at 159pm and the Ketchikan tide gauge topped out at 55mph at 206pm. The roof wind at the Ketchikan Airport on Gravina Island had a peak gust of 63mph at 153pm.

COOP observer at the northern end of Ketchikan, near Port Higgins, estimated winds of 40-65mph between 2-6am on the 22nd and checked the damaging wind box. Peak wind gusts elsewhere in the borough were measured at 44-53mph.

The Alaska Marine Highway Ferry Columbia could not dock as scheduled on the morning of the 26th due to winds and seas. The Inter Island Ferry was cancelled for the day in anticipation of the storm. There were several flight cancellations in and out of Ketchikan due to the wind. A ship report in a cove on the north side of Gravina Island estimated 60mph winds at 1250pm. Peak winds at other mesonet stations in the area ranged from 46 to 53 mph.

Mesonet station at Salmon Landing in Ketchikan reported a maximum wind gust of 63 mph at 1232pm on the 15th. In addition, the State Ferry Columbia was unable to dock in Ketchikan for a period of time, and the scheduled flight from Sitka to Ketchikan was unable to land, both due to high winds.

Light snow fell overnight, but quickly became moderate to heavy with several inches stacking up between 6 to 9am. Greatest amounts were reported with social media during the 8am hour, including 6 to 8 inches on the south side of Ketchikan. The band of snow showers shifted north of the area by noon.

The Marine Exchange station at Saxman measured a peak gust of 62 mph at 853am AKST  on Wednesday the 6th. Other observation sites in the are reported peak gusts of 45-55 mph between 7am and 11am that morning. The Ketchikan Indian Community and Tribal Health Clinic reported the high winds were causing doors to be dangerously ripped open.

The Metlakatla area saw an extended period of high winds starting early on the 9th of November. The mesonet station at the Annette Island Packing Company measured a peak gust of 79mph at 330am AKST. The Metlakatla AWOS topped out at 55mph between 455 and 536am. Another mesonet station at Walden Point Rd, near the ferry terminal, measured a peak gust of 63mph at 215pm AKST. At elevation, Yellow Hill peaked at 91mph during this event.

The peak wind measured at the Annette Island Packing Company in Metlakatla was 61mph in the 9am AKDT hour on the 26th. Other peak winds measured at higher elevations on the island ranged from 65 to 74mph.
The station at the Annette Island Packing Company measured a peak gust of 59.8mph at 433am AKDT. Other reports at upper elevations from around Annette Island ranged from 71 to 83mph.

The mesonet station located at the Annette Island Packing Company, located along the shoreline of Metlakatla, started to measure wind gusts in excess of 60mph at 140am on the 26th and continued through that afternoon, including a peak gust of 80mph at 425am. Other high wind gusts were measured at the elevation sites of Yellow Hill and Melson Lake. A NWS Employee reported that two power poles were leaning over or snapped on Walden Point Rd, closing the road and nearby stores. A later report from the local tribal government indicated damage had occurred to the historic Boat House.

Mesonet stations across Annette Island measured high winds for approximately two hours on the 15th. The Packing Company measured peak gusts of 62 mph at 1035pm and the Yellow Hill Station, at 479 ft elevation, reported a peak gust of 83 mph at 1230pm.

Light snow quickly became moderate to heavy with several inches stacking up between 6 to 9am. NWS Annette Island measured 6.7 inches had fallen at the Ferry Terminal by 848am on the 3rd. Amounts were lower in town.

Tuntutuliak Public Safety Office reported several houses close to the river were filled with water.  Conditions reportedly Worse than Merbok, with more water and stronger wind/waves. A boat was reported to be overturned in the river by wind/waves; it later sunk.

Napakiak City Office reported water over the roads coinciding with high tide. Water moved gravel along and off the street. Sloughs filled up along a road that runs between the city and airport, overrunning the road with water. Southwest winds during high tide further contributed toward higher water.  Water levels came up over the river banks with this system at about 2 and a half feet.

Nearly-persistent southerly winds led to storm surge and backed up flow, exacerbated by heavy rain, along the Kuskokwim River between August 15 and 18. Residents reported flooding and rapid bank erosion during high tides on August 16 and 17 at Akiak, Napakiak, Kasigluk, and Tuntutuliak. At Napakiak, a village elder reported the bank in front of the school was eroding rapidly and was only about 6 ft from the structure. Water inundated most low spots in the village, including the low spot in the road to the dump. Water levels were reported to be higher than during breakup flooding in May. A resident in Kasigluk reported water encroached on low lying residences, with similar water levels to this year's breakup and only a few inches lower than during Merbok in September 2022. The highest tide levels of the event occurred on August 18 as southerly winds gusted 50-55 mph into the Kuskokwim Del

NWS Riverwatch reported an ice jam had formed near Napakiak and the impounded water would be reported to flood most of the village of Napakiak.  The warning was rolled into an additional warning for the reach from Napakiak upstream to Bethel.  Widespread flooding of the tundra in addition to the villages along the Kuskokwim river would also be reported which caused flood waters to impound for longer periods of time without any path to drainage.

Riverwatch would report an ice jam had formed near Napakiak and was flooding communities upstream including Napaskiak and Oscarville.  The initial advisory was upgraded to a warning which covered the reach of the Kuskokwim River from Bethel downstream through Napakiak.  Widespread flooding to homes and transportation was reported in Oscarville and Napaskiak.

Initial flooding in Bethel and surrounding areas causes minor low land overflows and some impacted to transportation prompting an advisory, however flood intensity started to increase when the ice jam stalled downstream causing large amounts of impounded water to inundate well into Bethel.  The rising water triggered a flood warning to be issued for Bethel and the surrounding area as impacts included the area inside of Bethel called Alligator Acres being heavily flooded, as well as the bridge over Brown's Slough being impassible (where the gage is located).  The flooding had a strong impact on numerous businesses in the areas of Bethel along the Kuskokwim River and Brown's Slough.  Flooding was also reported spreading into the tundra in the countryside, flooding low roads and rural transportation in the area.

Due to an areawide internet outage, timing of snowfall is estimated based on automated snow depth sensors. The morning Klondike Highway report from DOT at 807am on the 28th noted difficult travel conditions and a range of 1 to 8 inches of snow between 12 mile and the border, and up to 6 inches between mile markers 8 to 12. This range of speeds may imply drifting snow and snow continued until later that afternoon. Another observation was not available, and total accumulation is unknown. Before observations dropped off at around 9pm on the 27th, the White Pass RWIS was gusting to 37mph.

Snow began late in the night on the 13th and became heavy through the early morning hours of the 14th, reaching 10 inches by 830am. Heavy snow continued through the mid-day with winds gusting to around 25mph and visibilities down to a half mile. By the time snow ended in the late afternoon, the total accumulation was 14.5 inches.

NWS employee in Yakutat measured 8.4 inches of snow the morning of the 29th for a daily CoCoRaHS report, but noted that most of that had fallen by late evening on the 28th. More rounds of heavy snow fell on the 29th with an additional 7.8 inches measured by the following morning.
The Yakutat ASOS station recorded wind gusts in excess of 60 mph for a 4 hour period during a frontal passage. This included a peak gust of 66 mph at 450pm.

Snow showers fell over Yakutat the evening of the 3rd through the early morning with reports ranging from 5 to 6.4 inches across town. Snow began again in the late morning but accumulation rates were lower with only an additional 1 to 2.4 inches falling by the following morning.

A past NWS Employee estimated 6 to 8 inches of dry fluffy snow by 815am on the 27th. The WSO confirmed 7.1 inches by 845am with only a trace of additional accumulation falling through the rest of the day. The Yakutat airport was reporting gusts of 20-25 mph and visibility down to a half mile at times.

Unalaska Roads Department reported heavy rain in Unalaska washed out several gravel roadways in the surrounding area.  Blocked culverts caused additional street flooding and also washed large crevasses up to 4 ft deep in some of the roadways.

Unalaska experienced multiple mudslides and flooding over non-primary roadways, including Ballyhoo Road where road access was restricted.  Mudslides along roadways did require fire department response.

A mariner reported that a waterspout developed between Cheval Island and Pony Cove starting around 10:45 AM AKST that moved from west to east after developing and lasted for about 5 minutes.  Photo evidence provided by this mariner showed a clear funnel cloud and surface circulation kicking up sea spray.  While this waterspout developed close to several islands, there was no clear evidence this feature ever reached land before it dissipated.

Snow Glacial Dam releases caused minor flooding along the Kenai River from near Seward to Skilak Lake.  Water levels reached minor flood levels, with reports of high water closing down boat access, reaching into yards, and encroaching garages that were along the river.

Heavy rains across Cordova, AK increased river levels quickly causing areas of minor flooding and lowland overflows in the area. Eyak Lake showed a rapid rise to minor flood stage, however, impacts were limited to flooding along low lying areas and along low roadways. The Eyak Lake river gage crested at 4.81 ft. Portions of the Copper River Highway, connecting Cordova to the airport, had been washed away according to the Cordova Police Department.

A suspected freeze-up ice jam on the Tanana River near Harding Lake resulted in overflow and flooding along Sewell Drive. Water inundated private property at two residences and a portion of Sewell Drive was flooded. One resident had 5 inches of water in their home. Many personal items and equipment surrounding the residences were partially submerged in the floodwaters. Water slowly receded after peaking on around December 2nd.

Report with video showing a dugout at a ballfield in Petersburg being blown over at 304pm on the 26th. Another report from social media later that day of trees coming down near 9 mile Mitkof Highway, including a photo of a pine tree on a home. The report also said that the power was out with trees on the lines. The Petersburg COOP, located at the airport, checked the damaging wind box and measured a peak gust of 42kt at 406pm AKDT.

Weather observer at the Petersburg Airport had 5 inches of snow by 1pm on the 30th and noted 2 inches from the day before. Periods of heavy snow continued through the evening of the 30th, but was swept away by the wind, making it difficult to measure.

Snow began to fall at the Petersburg airport at 1130am on the 1st and the COOP there measured 6 inches of snow by 9pm. A trained spotter near 9 mile Mitkof Highway measured a total of 7.5 inches the next morning.

Media in Petersburg reported that a 3 foot diameter spruce tree came down Sunday night, blocking both lanes of the Mitkof Highway near Blaquerie Point. During this period, a peak gust of 66mph was measured at the Zarembo Island RAWS, at 155am.

Light snow fell during the MLK long weekend across Petersburg with heaviest rates falling on the 15th when the COOP at the airport measured 11.5 inches. This in addition to the snowfall measured the previous 2 days gave a storm total of 16.9 inches. A period of freezing rain was also noted by the airport observer toward the end of the event. A trained spotter called in 7 inches of snow fell over a 12 hour period during the heaviest rates while a social media post shared that 12.5 inches had fallen near Crystal Lake Hatchery.

Reports were received that a storm blew trees onto Mitkof Highway and snapped two power poles near the Crystal Lake Hydroelectric Plant. The bulk of the damage occurred between 3 and 18 mile Mitkof Highway. around approximately 12:30 PM AKDT (11:30 AM AKST). Customers in that area were without power on Easter Sunday for more than 5 hours.

recent.narrative: A trained spotter in Kake reported that rain changed to snow at about 940am on the 15th with visibility falling to a half mile. The spotter measured 4.5 inches by 249pm with heavy rates continuing. Another spotter SW of Kake in Security Bay reported similar conditions with a measurement of 8 inches and reported it had changed back to rain at 335pm. The change over to rain in Kake happened about an hour later with precipitation ending shortly after.

recent.area: WESTERN KUPREANOF ISLAND AND KUIU ISLAND
recent.narrative: A trained spotter in Security Bay, SW of Kake, reported 9.5 inches of snow already by 11am on the 27th along with blowing and drifting snow. The spotter reported another 6 inches by 11pm and another 3 inches the following morning for a total of 18.5 inches. A spotter in Kake reported 8-12 inches of snow by 8am on the 28th with significant drifting. The Kake airport was reporting wind gusts of around 20 mph and visibility down to three quarters of a mile at times.

recent.area: WESTERN KUPREANOF ISLAND AND KUIU ISLAND
recent.narrative: Trained spotter in Security Bay reported light snow fell on January 31st, but rates were below warning criteria. Snow continued to fall through the morning of the 1st with around 6 inches falling in a 12 hour period. Including snow from the previous day, the spotter measured 10.25 inches and was still snowing lightly at their 1144am observation time with a heavy snow load on trees. The nearest community of Kake continued to report snow until the 8pm hour, but no snowfall reports from that area.

recent.area: WESTERN KUPREANOF ISLAND AND KUIU ISLAND
recent.narrative: A trained spotter in Security Bay, SW of Kake, received 6 inches of wet snow by 7am on the 20th. At 3pm the total was up to 16 inches and changed to heavy rain. No reports were received from the community of Kake or Port Alexander.

recent.area: WESTERN KUPREANOF ISLAND AND KUIU ISLAND
recent.narrative: A trained spotter in Security Bay reported 8.5 inches of snow. The spotter later reported that the snow had changed to rain by 4 PM AKDT. Another spotter in Port Alexander estimated 8 inches of snow had fallen by 830am on the 15th.

recent.area: WESTERN KUPREANOF ISLAND AND KUIU ISLAND
recent.narrative: Trained spotter in Security Bay, 17 miles W of Kake, measured 8.5 inches of snow by 1038am on the 1st. A change to rain occurred after this time.
The City of Ambler city office reported a foot of snow fell in a 24 hour period.
Ambler AWOS had numerous hours of moderate or heavy snow with half mile visibility or less at times.
An automated sensor near Kiana reported 10 inches of snow within 24 hours.

The main flow of the Sagavanirktok (Sag) River was diverted to the farthest west channel of the river due to aurfeis blocking the channel. The Sag River was pushed up against the Dalton Highway and began to erode the road near Milepost 403.5. On June 7th the road was closed at Milepost 403.5 due to the Sag River eroding the highway to the centerline with the threat of a total washout. This closure shut off the only road access to the oil fields on the North Slope of Alaska. The AK Department of Transportation immediately began hauling rock from a quarry 150 miles away in order to secure the road. The road reopened to one lane traffic on June 8th, although the threat of erosion continued for another week. Runoff from heavy rain and snowmelt in the headwaters of the Sag River reached Milepost 403.5 of the Dalton Highway on June 14th.

C218.name: S. SLOPES OF ERN BROOKS RANGE

recent.area: S. SLOPES OF ERN BROOKS RANGE
recent.narrative: Water levels rose rapidly on the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River on Friday June 9th and went overbank and caused minor flooding by Saturday morning June 10th. At Wiseman, residents reported approximately 3 inches of water over the lower part of the access road into Wiseman. The high water caused bank erosion and some erosion on the Wiseman Road surface. High groundwater levels also caused flooding of the crawl space in at least one home in Wiseman along Wiseman Creek.

A social media post from around 2pm AKDT reported damage to a board walk at Warm Springs Bay on the eastern side of Baranof Island. The Sitka Airport ASOS measured a gust of 54kt (62mph) at 347pm AKDT and a peak gust of 58kt (67mph) at 356pm AKDT. The COOP station at Little Port Walter checked the damaging wind box for this event.

The ferry M/V Columbia traveling through Peril Strait, along the northern border of the zone, measured a peak gust out of the east of 52kt at 645am AKDT. Peak winds measured at the Sitka Airport ASOS was  46mph after winds shifted to the SW.||Based on the sting jet hitting the outer coast of Baranof and Kruzof Islands, expect tree damage to unpopulated areas.

The Sitka Airport ASOS measured a peak gust of 60mph at 446am AKDT Wednesday the 17th. A local weather spotter noted some small branches and twigs blown off trees, trash cans and plastic chairs blown over, and a previously damaged store front window now broken with glass on the sidewalk downtown. A tug boat traveling through Peril Strait, north of Sitka, measured a peak gust of 67kt at 617am AKDT.
The ASOS at the Sitka airport on Japonski Island measured high wind gusts over 60 mph early on Saturday October 12th. The strongest gust was 66 mph at 120am AKDT.

The Sitka Airport measured gusts of 30-50mph through the morning of the 27th, then continued gusts of 20-30mph through the rest of the day a visibility briefly down to a quarter mile at times. Trained spotters reported variable snowfall amounts due to blowing and drifting snow in the morning of the 27th. Through the morning of the 28th, an estimated 8.25 inches of snow had fallen.

A burst of high winds were felt across Sitka during the morning hours of the 29th. A peak gust of 71 mph was recorded by the Sitka ASOS at 910am and a peak gust of 78 mph was measured at the Marine Exchange station at the Sitka Harbor at 1013am. Additionally numerous reports were received of down trees all over town.
An RWIS station just over 3 miles from the border with Hyder recorded around 12.5 inches of snow between 11am on the 28th and 2am on the 29th.

Snow began shortly before midnight on the 1st. A Hyder resident called that afternoon to report that 7 inches had fallen so far and was continuing to snow. Snow changed to rain the following morning and the nearby town of Stewart B.C. measured 13.4 inches overnight.

Snow began late on February 28th and became heavy through the following morning and continued for approximately 24 hours. The COOP in Hyder measured 2.8 inches of snow by 4am and noted rates of 2 inches per hours shortly after. The nearby town of Stewart B.C. recorded heavy ice pellets at 921am and snow continuing through 11pm.
COOP Observer in Hyder measured 11.7 inches of dry powdery snow at 330am Saturday the 25th and was still falling at a moderate rate at the time. COOP noted snow began around noon on Friday the 24th.

COOP Observer in Hyder measured 2.8 inches of snow early on the 15th and another 12.6 inches had fallen by the following morning. Nearby Stewart B.C. observation site measured over 9 inches of snow by 4pm AKST on the 15th and was still snowing moderately.

Report from a local Wrangell radio station of a roof torn off a building in the 5am AKDT hour on the 17th. A later post with photos by the owner showed an external snow roof rolled up with all material stripped away. Peak winds measured at the Wrangell Airport ASOS during the storm was 45mph.

Reports on social media were received of new snowfall in Wrangell of 8+ inches of new snowfall. One report indicated that as of 8pm on the 28th that 12 inches of snow had fallen, with eight inches of that to have fallen since noon. Another trained spotter south of town measured 10 inches by 10pm and reported it as very dense and heavy. Snow ending time is estimated.

A trained spotter south of Wrangell measured 4 inches of snow by 8am on the 27th with 1 mile visibility. By 7pm their total was up to 6.5 inches. Intermittent moderate snowfall continued through the night with another 2 inches falling, but the total compressing down to 7.25 inches. The Wrangell airport observer measured periodic gusts of 20-30 mph during the day on the 27th and visibility down to a quarter mile briefly.

Light snow fell during the MLK long weekend across Wrangell with heaviest rates falling on the 15th between 10am and 10pm. A trained spotter measured 14 inches storm total by late evening and others on social media confirmed that amount the next day.

Report of a downed tree at approximately 130pm, in the power line at 5.5 mile Zimovia Highway and another tree town at 6.5 mile. Trained spotter also reported the outage. Winds on nearby Zarembo Island saw a peak gust of 68 mph at 255pm. A second power outage was reported at 320pm with a tree down across 8 mile Zimovia Highway.

Snow began late on February 28th and became heavy through the following morning with periodic gusts of around 30mph. A change to rain happened in the late morning. A trained spotter south of Wrangell measured 6 inches of dense snow.

A Marine Exchange of Alaska sensor at the southern tip of Admiralty Island, Point Garner, measured wind gusts in excess of 60mph for several hours, including a peak gust of 65.6kt at 210pm AKDT. Warming temperatures caused dense snowpack above the town of Glennallen to rapidly melt sending a large volume of water into the town of Glennallen.  A flood watch was issued as early as April 28, with the advisory covering the more severe flooding from the snowmelt.  By May 2, the advisory was issued to address flooding specifically along Trooper Creek and Moose Creek.  Water had flooded into the fire station (reports noted 10 inches of water in the VFD station) and surrounded the legislative office. Additionally, flooding had proven numerous local roads impassable with flooding noted across other low-lying areas across Glennallen. By May 6, flooding had expanded to close Snowshoe Drive which impacted transportation across the town. Late season snow in the Moose Creek Basin rapidly melted at the beginning of June 2023 causing another episode of flooding in the Glennallen area.  While not as severe as the May flood event, the June event flooded the Glennallen Library and closed Glenn Highway due to highwater.

Snowmelt flooding pushed the Gulkana River to moderate flood levels on May 21-22, 2023.  Flooding of lowland areas and impacts to locations such as the Sourdough Campground led to flood advisory issuance.  Richardson Highway was surrounded by high water and travelers in the region were notified of threats in the region.
Department of Transportation reported rapid snowmelt is occurring, and is causing minor flooding with water over portions of the Old Edgerton Highway near the Richardson Highway.

Snowmelt flooding pushed Moose Creek into flood across Glennallen, AK.  The flood inundated the town of Glennallen, flooding homes, businesses and Glenn Highway at MP 185, forcing it to close.  Flooding was extensive and a disaster declaration was declared for Glennallen on May 13, 2023 for the severe flooding.

Borderline Red Flag Warning criteria was met at the Gulkana ASOS from around 4 pm to 8 pm AKDT. Temperatues hovered near 75 degrees Fahrenheit with sustained northerly winds of 13 to 16 mph with a peak gust of 25 mph. Relative humidity ranged from 25% to 29% during this same time period.

Additionally, travel was severely hampered for the duration of the snow event as areas along the Richardson Hwy, including Thompson Pass, were closed due to heavy snow. Additionally, a Borough Official reported a storm total snow amount of 16 inches at 0800 January 29th in McCarthy, a town affected by the road closures.

From AK 511 (DOT) reported that the Richardson Hwy from MP 30 to MP 42 as of 6:56AM 12/11/23 had very difficult travel conditions with blowing and drifting snow, icy patches and packed snow on roadways. The DOT warned of possible road closure with travel not advised. Snow of 6 to 10 inches was reported.

Alaska DOT reported black ice and icy roads along the Richardson Highway south of Kenny Lake on November 23 and 24. Conditions were classed as Hazardous on November 24. The Gulkana ASOS also reported unknown precipitation at 31 degrees on the morning of November 24, indicating light freezing rain also affected more central portions of the Copper River Basin as well. Temperatures warmed above freezing that evening with the arrival of a southerly Copper River wind.
The Richardson Highway was closed around 2 PM from Thompson Pass north due to 'hazardous' road conditions and very heavy snowfall with the  D.O.T reporting 72 inches of storm total snowfall.

The station reported a max wind gust for three consecutive observations from 3:11 PM AKST to 3:21 PM AKST on January 25th. Other weather stations in the area reported similarly high gusts of over 70 mph around the same timeframe. Wind gusts over the Anchorage International Airport exceeded 60 mph on January 25th.

The Potter Valley and Arctic Valley weather stations (PMHA2 and ARCA2) reported wind gusts of over 80 mph for an extended period of time during the morning hours of January 12th. Arctic Valley was especially gusty and experience a wind gust of 107 mph at 11:00 AM AKST before the station stopped reported data. Other weather stations around these areas similarly reported strong wind gusts over 80 mph around the same time period. An NWS employee reported a 73 mph wind gusts at the site GW5352 ANCHORAGE, which resulted in a door to his shed being blown down. An article from Alaska Public Media reported many impacts across Anchorage including structure damage, downed powerlines which led to power outages, and down trees. A weather station (PMHA2) on the Anchorage Hillside reported a peak wind gust of 82 mph at 12:52 AM AKST January 7th. More gusts of over 70 mph were reported by this same station for the next 30 minutes afterwards. Other stations nearby reported wind gusts exceeding 70 mph near the same time period. Winds peaked just after midnight as the low moved inland and pressure began to rise.

The Anchorage ASOS Station (PANC) reported freezing rain at 12:07 PM AKST 1/6/25. PAMR and PAED similarly reported freezing rain near the same time period. Posts from social media reported graupel, freezing rain, rain, and snow. A trained spotter reported 0.1 inches of snowfall on the Anchorage Hillside. Ekluna Lake Rd closed at 12:40 PM AKST January 6th due to an extreme ice buildup and unsafe road conditions. An employee from the River Forecast Center shared a report that said The road is an unholy mess and cars are piling up at mile 4 and 4.5. Eklutna Lake Road is currently blocked by stranded cars - people can't get up or down. There were numerous social media reports of accidents and cars sliding off roads in Anchorage and Eagle River. An Anchorage police spokesperson said that 79 accidents and 54 vehicles in distress had been reported Monday January 6th.

A CWOP weather station on the Anchorage Hillside reported a maximum wind gust of 81 mph at 3:17 PM AKST Dec 9th. Other observation sites in the sane area reported wind gusts between 60 to 75 mph at around the same time. Wind gusts remained elevated between 60 and 70 mph in the Hillside over the course of the day and into Tuesday Dec 10th until around 8:00 AM. The lower elevations had wind gusts between 45 to 55 mph until around 7:00 PM Monday. There were reports on social media of siding being ripped off a home in Ft. Richardson as well as a broken window and a minor injury. A large tree snapped and fell on a power line in the Spenard area sometime on Monday, leaving 1800 customers without power in the Chugach Electric Service area and 1300 without power in the Matanuska Electric service area by 9:30 PM that same day.

NWS employees reported slick back roads across Anchorage the morning of December 5th. Ice accumulated on trees, bushes, and power lines on the south edge of Midtown. Temperatures dropped below freezing overnight December 5th into December 6th which prompted refreezing of water on roadways, creating additional slick road conditions.

An ice jam formed on the Kobuk River below Kobuk on May 18th. Minor flooding caused caused water to inundate low lying roads, around and partially under three homes, making some areas in the community on accessible by boat. Water levels started to gradually fall on the 20th and it is estimated the ice jam released on the 21st when water levels dropped back within back at the community.

recent.narrative: The Alaska Department of Transportation closed Thompson Pass from Milepost 12 to Milepost 46 at 8:00 AM AKST January 26th due to avalanche danger and inclement weather. The Department of Transportation 511 website reported Very Difficult road conditions the same day.

Blizzard conditions occurred in Whittier (WMHA2) between 9:00 AM and 12:00 PM AKST on January 12th. Winds gusted to over 60 mph with visibility dropping to a quarter of a mile during this timeframe until the weather sensor failed. There were also reports of heavy snow and winds along portions of the Seward Highway the same day.

A SNOTEL in Turnagain Pass reported snowfall rates of more than 2 inches per hour in the early morning hours of November 5th. There were reports from social media that near-whiteout conditions were occurring along the Seward Highway near Turnagain Pass during the same time period.
The Turnagain Pass SNOTEL recorded an increase of 9 inches of snow depth on 2/9, ending at 9 PM AKST.

Spotters from the Chugach National Forest Avalanche Information Center (CNFAIC) reported 20 inches of snow fell at road level through Turnagain Pass on Jan 7. The snow line was between 600 and 800 ft, meaning precipitation that fell through the pass was likely all snow. No wind information was available.

Whittier MAWS reported visibility one half mile or lower with winds gusting in excess of 31 knots (36 mph) on the morning of December 12 through shortly after noon. Similar visibilities were observed at Portage Glacier during the same time period.

The Portage ASOS Station (PATO) reported strong winds that frequently gusted to over 70 mph for a four hour period between 8:00 AM to 12:00 PM AKST on January 12th. Other stations around the same area reported similar wind speeds in the same timeframe. Alyeska Resort had even higher winds with  gusts over 100 mph from 4:00 AM to 9:00 AM AKST the same day. An article from Alaska Public Media reported that Alyeska Resort closed, citing extreme winds, downed trees, and debris on the slopes which make conditions unsafe for skiing and snowboarding. Link to the Alaska Public article: https://alaskapublic.org/news/anchorage/2025-01-13/you-cant-sit-and-relax-anchorage-cleans-up-after-turbulent-winds.

The Portage ASOS (PATO) reported a wind gust measuring 82 mph at 12:31 PM AKST January 6th. Weather stations at Alyeska Resort reported wind gusts of over 90 mph around the same time. High winds led to the closure of Alyeska Resort due to a power outage. An animal shelter at the Alaska Wildlife Conservation Center was destroyed by high winds.

An ASOS station in Portage (PATO) reported a maximum wind gust of 85 mph on Monday, Dec 9th at 6:23 AM AKST. Several other stations reported wind gusts in the 50s and 60s including a peak gust of 69 mph in Whittier (WHMA2). Wind gusts remained elevated at around 45 to 55 mph, particularly in Whittier, until around 2:00 PM Dec 9th.
The observation at PATO: 8:53am W 7G25 and ended at 12:53pm.
Periods of heavy snow reduced visibilities to near zero along Seward Highway near Turnagain Pass.

An RWIS/DOT observation site in Portage reported 2 to 3 hours of moderate to heavy snow with visibility under 1 mile between 9 PM AKST 12/7 and 12 AM ASKST 12/8 with winds gusting from the west between 20 and 35 mph.

Ice jam flooding started late at night on May 12th and when the Riverwatch team landed in Eagle on May 13th (early afternoon) flood waters had receded leaving stranded ice well above the bank. The USGS river gage had a preliminary crest of 42 feet at 5 AM ADT on May 13th. Moderate flood impacts included damage to the seawall with the guardrail along the seawall was destroyed, stranded ice, and flooding on the road between Eagle and Eagle Village leaving the road impassable for a week due to stranded ice. Several structures in town were damaged by ice and floodwaters, including the Falcon Inn which had a high water mark of almost 2 feet into the finished basement. Preceding the ice jam, the river was at or above bank full, with Mission Road beginning to flood late afternoon of May 12th.||Prior to the Eagle event, there were multiple significant ice jams in Canada, including a 30-mile-long

An ice jam formed on the Mosquito Fork of the Fortymile River approximately 1.5 miles downstream from the Taylor Highway bridge. A NWS automated river gage on the bridge recorded a rise in water levels of 10 feet in 48 hours. Ice rose to the base of the bridge and lower part of the guardrail but damage to the bridge was not observed. Water also went overbank and flooded portions of a wayside at the bridge but the Taylor Highway was not impacted by floodwaters and the road remained open.

Water levels on the Koyukuk River at Allakaket rose overbank in low-lying areas of the community near the river on June 10th. Minor flooding was reported when the water crested early Monday morning June 12th. Water inundated the old runway by the river and overtopped Stanley Slough Road near the boat launch. A local observer reported that the high water and debris was initially coming from the Alatna River on June 10th but then coming down the Koyukuk River by June 11th. It is estimated water levels would need to rise approximately 1 additional foot to go over roads in the lower part of the village and have more significant impacts.

Salmon River reported an increase in snow depth of 9.6 inches in 24 hours, with a storm total accumulation of 13.7 inches.

Z807.name: HOWARD PASS AND THE DELONG MOUNTAINS

recent.area: HOWARD PASS AND THE DELONG MOUNTAINS
recent.narrative: High winds developed during the afternoon hours at the Lisburne Hills USARRAY site (C16KX). Wind gusts up to 69 mph were reported.

The Pilgrim Hot Springs SNOTEL site (PHSA2) located in the higher terrain of the southwestern Seward Peninsula experienced almost 48 hours of steady heavy snowfall. 8 inches of new snow was reported in the first 24 hours with a 48 hour total of 13 new snowfall.
SNOTEL data from the Seward Peninsula at Paragon Creek reported total snowfall of 8 with additional light snow still falling.
A public weather station reported wind gusts as high as 61 mph along the Taylor Highway north of Nome.
High winds developed during the afternoon hours at the Hoodoo Hills (HDOA2). Wind gusts up to 62 mph were reported.

An ice jam formed in the Lower Yukon River upstream of Hill Island, on Saturday, May 18th. Water levels at Pilot Station rose slowly with water overbank and flooding roads in the lower portions of the village. As of early evening Saturday, May 18th, water surrounded the tribal office, AC store, tribal store and as many as 5 houses. At 330 pm Sunday, May 19th, trained river spotters reported the ice jam on the Yukon River downstream of Pilot Station released. Water levels were receding at Pilot Station due to the ice jam releasing by the morning of May 20th. A Flood Watch was issued on May 18th and upgraded to a Flood Warning on May 18th. The Flood Warning was cancelled on May 20th.

Widespread coastal flooding was reported across Diomede and Shishmaref as strong winds pushed water onshore. Diomede lost power and Alaska Energy Authority (AEA) was engaged. Two shipping containers were floated by the storm. Tribal elders in Shishmaref reported the worst high water in memory. Severe shoreline erosion was reported on the north and south end of town. The village's protective berm was damaged.  Roads and the landfill were damaged, an archeological site was lost due to erosion, one outbuilding floated. Graves were swept away.
Water began rising during the morning hours of the 3rd. Minor flooding of low-lying areas was observed in Golovin, including the old runway.

Through the late morning hours of September 15th reports from the local emergency manager reported significant runoff from the steep hillside that surrounds the Ketchikan area from the very heavy rain. This overland flow continued and increased into the afternoon, which flooded numerous roads that had to be closed due to the depth of water and the risk to life and property to the drivers. Some of this urban flooding did occur in poor drainage areas, during the tourist season, and affected traffic and the safety of the visitors. In the afternoon, the emergency manager reported brown water in the runoff, causing elevated concern for landslides, although no landslides were recorded from this event. Shortly after 1500AKST on August 25th the larger of two landslides crossed the 3rd Avenue Bypass, a state road which is one of two routes for local traffic to get across town. There were 2 city employees that were working to clear culverts in their vehicle as the landslide occurred and killed the driver and significantly injuring the other passenger. As the landslide progressed down the slope, it destroyed 5 houses, caused 2 additional injuries, and damage to other surrounding properties. The entire area around the slide was evacuated until the hillside was evaluated. The 3rd AVE Bypass was closed and produced major congestion due to summer tourism as there was only one main road to move through town and this made it difficult for emergency services to get around in a timely fashion.

The second landslide, on the opposite slope of the first, went down Copper Ridge and affected a private construction yard. Construction materials stored at the yard were destroyed in the slide, which was significant loss, along with the damage/destruction of the upper part of the access road.
